Algebra. The branch of mathematics concerned with operations on abstract symbols and the relationships between quantities. Rather than working solely with concrete numbers, algebra uses variables to represent unknowns and develops systematic methods for manipulating equations and expressions.

The term derives from al-jabr, an Arabic word meaning reunion of broken parts, reflecting its origins in ninth-century Persian mathematics with mathematicians like Al-Khwarizmi formalizing algebraic procedures. Algebra distinguishes between elementary algebra—manipulating variables and solving equations—and abstract algebra, which studies algebraic structures like groups, rings, and fields. Fundamental concepts include variables, constants, operations like addition and multiplication, and equations that express relationships between quantities. Working with these abstractly reveals universal truths invisible in numeric computation alone.

The fundamental theorem of algebra guarantees that any polynomial equation of degree n has exactly n complex roots, counting multiplicity. This cornerstone result ensures equations always have solutions in the complex numbers. Algebraic thinking involves recognizing patterns and generalizing them, replacing specific numbers with variables to discover universal rules that apply across infinitely many cases.

Algebra is used in nearly every scientific and engineering discipline to model phenomena and predict outcomes, from physics and conservation laws to cryptography and machine learning. Solving for unknowns, reducing complex problems to simpler equations, is one of humanity's greatest intellectual achievements, enabling everything from bridge design to drug development. Historical algebra evolved through stages: geometric with the Greeks, algorithmic with the Arabs, symbolic in Renaissance Europe, and formal in the modern era, each stage revealing deeper structures and expanding algebraic reach.

Modern algebra extends far beyond solving equations, encompassing group theory, ring theory, field theory, and category theory—abstract structures revealing that many seemingly different mathematical objects share hidden symmetries.
